context: Biomes are broad living landscapes: forest, grassland, desert, tundra, and coast, set by climate and water more than by towns. Plants and the ground underfoot tell you which pattern you are in. A biome is not a line you can pace to a city limit. Weather still changes inside it.

Terrain is the shape you walk: flat, rolling, steep, broken, swampy, or cliffed. Steep ground costs time. Broken rock hides ankles. Soft ground hides depth. Choose the line that keeps you on ground you can see. This is a travel cue, not a soil survey or a road map.

A watershed is the land that drains to one stream, lake, or coast. Ridges are the divides. Water runs away from them into the basin. Following a creek downhill moves you toward that basin's trunk stream, not necessarily toward help. A drainage is not a trail.

A coast is where land meets a large body of water. Tides, cliffs, and headlands change the walkable strip through the day. A headland is a natural landmark. A harbor town is not stored here. Stay off wet rock when the sea is rising, and do not guess a tide table you do not have.

Mountains stack climate. Higher is usually colder, windier, and slower. A pass is a low saddle between higher ground. A peak is a landmark only while you can still see it. Weather arrives fast on ridges. Turn back when the route you can see runs out. This is not a climb grade.

Deserts are water-poor landscapes, hot or cold, where shade and the water you carry matter more than speed. Washes can flood from rain you do not see. Walk the firm edge of a wash, not its throat. Do not chase a shimmer toward a town. Night can turn sharply cold.

Forests hide the sun and the distant ridge. Travel is slower, and a handrail such as a stream or a ridge matters more than a bearing you cannot check. Moss is not a compass. Mark the way back while the last sure point is still in sight. This is not a timber or trail catalog.

Arctic and tundra country is open, cold, and often wet underfoot, with few trees to use as landmarks. When the horizon disappears, a short bearing and a counted pace are safer than a long walk. Summer light can last all day. Winter dark does the opposite. Ice is not a path this note approves.

River cues: a V of ripples often points at a rock, and smooth dark water can be deep. The outside of a bend cuts the bank. The inside piles gravel. Current is a force, not a trail. Wade only at a wide shallow place you have walked, and do not enter flood water.

Useful landmarks are natural and stable: a peak, a saddle, a lone butte, a confluence, a waterfall, a headland, a lake outlet. Name them on the map you carry and in a waypoint you save yourself. This store has no city, street, or business directory. If the landmark clouds over, rejoin a handrail.

Climate bands follow latitude and altitude in a rough way: tropical, subtropical, temperate, polar, plus dry belts where rain rarely falls. A band says what the season tends to do, not what tomorrow's storm will do. Height can copy a colder band. Watch the sky you actually have.

Magnetic declination is the angle between magnetic north and true north at a place. It changes slowly over years and with where you stand. A compass needle points magnetic. A map's meridians are the true frame. Set the declination printed on your map before you trust a bearing. There is no live declination feed.

True north follows the planet's axis, toward the geographic pole. Magnetic north is where the needle points, and the gap between them is declination. East declination means magnetic north sits east of true north. Add east declination to a magnetic bearing to plot true. A position lock is a point, not a north reference.

Contour lines join points of equal elevation. Lines close together mean steep ground. Wide gaps mean flatter ground. A V in the contours often points upstream in a valley. Index contours are the labeled ones. They show shape, not a trail name. The interval is printed on the map you carry.

Map and compass: set the map to the land, lay the compass edge on the line you mean to walk, turn the housing to north on the map, then turn your body until the needle agrees. Walk a short leg to a landmark you named and count paces. This is a method sketch, not a course certificate.

Elevation is height above a datum, often mean sea level. A GPS altitude, when a consented fix includes one, is a rough height and is weaker than the horizontal fix. If the lock has no altitude, say so and do not invent one. Contours show shape. A barometer drifts with the weather.

A great-circle course is the shortest path on a sphere between two latitudes and longitudes. The initial bearing is the direction you start, and it can change as you travel. Reverse bearing is the direction back. These tools use that spherical estimate. They do not follow roads and they do not download tiles.

A track log is a list of your own points, saved on this device only after you consent. Distance is the sum of the great-circle legs. Elapsed time is counted only when those points carry timestamps. It is not someone else's path, and it is not sent anywhere unless you say so in your own words.

Landscape navigation here is terrain, water, coast, and sky: distance, bearing, waypoints, and a track you record yourself. It deliberately has no city map, no street list, and no points of interest that go stale as towns change. If you need a town, use a map you brought, not this store.
